# Sequence 09 The cube lantern
[SourceLocator] Production sequence reference CH01-09. The following location descriptions are retained from V16.
### Lantern Street Cube Plinth, Handle and Moonline Joint
[SceneInstruction] A low square plinth under an indigo canopy stands opposite the mirror. The five-indicator wall control and large down-pull handle are on its right. One flat brass cover lies in the paving at the plinth’s front-right corner, over the moonline joint.
[SceneInstruction] Sixty-four small lantern cubes form one solid 4 × 4 × 4 block between the square base and top frame. The failed state is uneven narrow towers. An exact layer diagram shows sixteen cubes, then four layers. The final handle stays separate from the floor cover. Under that cover are two disconnected track ends, screws and black dust; there is no hidden second switch. The joint repair, not another calculation, makes the final light flow.
[SceneInstruction] Required views. Medium plinth; exact single layer and complete cube inserts; hand-on-handle still; low disconnected/connected joint views; result wide belongs to Lantern Street.
## Scene CH01 09A A lantern that cannot close
[SourceLocator] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[SceneInstruction] Setting. Lantern Street cube plinth and final control. A low square plinth beneath an indigo canopy stands opposite the mirror. The five-indicator wall control and large down-pull handle are on its right. A separate flat brass cover in the paving at the plinth’s front-right corner hides the right-edge moonline joint. Blue wall, canopy post and paving seam fix the geography. Same full-moon night in Mumbai. Warm fixed work lamps and the portable brass lamp make faces and hands readable; cool moonlight edges roofs and canopy gaps. Main lantern arches remain dark unless this scene explicitly changes them.
[SceneInstruction] View. Medium from the lane facing the low square plinth opposite the mirror. The indigo canopy, right-hand five-light control and down-pull handle identify the location. The floor joint cover is at the plinth’s front-right corner.
[SceneInstruction] Cast and staging across the scene. Ahana has returned her sketchbook and pencil to her backpack and picked up the work lamp. She faces the square base and asks the edge-length question. Navya and Vihaan stand on either side of her, examining the uneven towers without climbing or reaching beneath them. Tara explains with her staff in hand. The broad helper waits to rebuild; Tez remains beside Ahana.
[SceneInstruction] Props and state progression. Inventory exactly 64 small lantern cubes, stacked in thin uneven towers within this one plinth. The square top frame cannot close. First four indicators white, CUBE dark. The final handle is raised; the brass floor cover remains closed and its disconnection unseen.
[SceneInstruction] Planning requirements. A distant tower view may conceal individual counts; the stated inventory is exact. No four-by-four layer or solved edge shown before T1.5. The final control and floor cover are separate objects.

[PrintLabel] Exact teaching text begins
[MathSection] 1.5 Cubes and Cube Roots
Our square tiles covered a flat surface. Now let’s build upwards too. We’ll find how much space a cube holds, then work backwards from that space to its side length. Start with small blocks, each 1 cm long, 1 cm wide and 1 cm high.
Put 2 blocks along and 2 blocks across to make one layer. That layer contains 2 × 2 = 4 blocks. Stack 2 such layers:
[Equation] 2 × 2 × 2 = 4 × 2 = 8 blocks
[SmallCaption] Two layers make a cube
[Production] Production note V11. Show a 2 by 2 layer of exactly four unit cubes, a second matching layer of four, and an assembled 2 by 2 by 2 cube. Use consistent labelled lower and upper layers. Show all three outer dimensions as 2 cm on the assembled cube. Identify a unit cube as 1 cm³. Hidden cubes still count; do not depict only the visible faces as the total. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
To cube a number, use three copies of it as factors. We call the result its cube and write a small raised 3:
[Equation] 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8
[Equation] 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = 125
2³ means 2 × 2 × 2, not 2 × 3. Our cube has 8 blocks, not 6.
Cubes of whole numbers are called perfect cubes. Cubing 1 to 10 gives 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729 and 1000. Zero is a perfect cube too: 0³ = 0.
The 2 cm cube has volume 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. cm³ means cubic centimetres: how many 1 cm by 1 cm by 1 cm cubes fit inside. A side is a length; volume counts the space inside the whole solid.
On a calculator: use x³ if your calculator has it, or the power key to enter 5³. You should get 125. If needed, 5 × 5 × 5 does the same calculation. Check which expression is on the display, since calculator keys differ.
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE074-PANEL01

[MathSubsection] Finding the side of a cube
Suppose a cube contains 27 unit blocks. What number of blocks goes along each edge? We need three copies of the same number that multiply to give 27.
[Equation] 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, so ∛27 = 3
The symbol ∛ means cube root. That little 3 on the root sign matters: it asks for three equal factors, not two.
[SmallCaption] Twenty seven blocks in three layers
[Production] Production note V12. Show a 3 by 3 by 3 cube with all face divisions aligned and three adjacent 3 by 3 layer plans. Each plan contains nine cells. Label 3 layers, 9 cubes per layer, volume 27 cm³ and edge 3 cm. The plans explain the hidden cubes rather than adding extra cubes to the solid. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Look at the three layer plans: 9 blocks in each of 3 layers give 27 blocks. So a cube of volume 27 cm³ has edge length 3 cm. Cubing finds the volume from the edge; a cube root finds the edge from the volume.
Similarly, ∛8 = 2 because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. On a calculator, use the cube-root function for ∛64; the answer should be 4. Check: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

[MathExample] Example 16
Evaluate (a) ∛8 + 2³, (b) ∛125 − 5³ and (c) ∛64 × 5 − 3³.
[AnswerLead] Let’s work it through
(a) The root and the cube are different instructions. ∛8 = 2, while 2³ = 8:
[Equation] ∛8 + 2³ = 2 + 8 = 10
(b) Here ∛125 = 5, while 5³ = 125. Subtracting the bigger amount gives a negative answer:
[Equation] ∛125 − 5³ = 5 − 125 = −120
(c) Find the root and the cube first. Then multiply before subtracting:
[Equation] ∛64 × 5 − 3³ = 4 × 5 − 27 = 20 − 27 = −7
The root bar covers 64 only. The × 5 stays outside it.

[Equation] (c) 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 16 × 4 = 64
[Equation] (d) 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = 125

[MathExample] 4 Evaluate
(a) 7³ − ∛8 (b) √64 − ∛64
(c) 2² × 4³ − ∛512 (d) 2³ − ∛343 − ∛27
[AnswerLead] Check your method
[Equation] (a) 7³ − ∛8 = 343 − 2 = 341
[Equation] (b) √64 − ∛64 = 8 − 4 = 4
[Equation] (c) 2² × 4³ − ∛512 = 4 × 64 − 8 = 256 − 8 = 248
[Equation] (d) 2³ − ∛343 − ∛27 = 8 − 7 − 3 = 1 − 3 = −2
In (b), both roots contain 64, but their instructions differ: 8 × 8 = 64, whereas 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

[AnswerLead] Check your method
Read what you are given and what you need in each picture:
First square: We know the area is 64 cm² and need the side, so write √64 cm. Check: 8 × 8 = 64, so the side is 8 cm.
Second square: Each side is 64 cm. To find the area, write 64² cm²: 64 × 64 = 4096.
First cube: We know the volume is 64 cm³ and need the side, so write ∛64 cm. Check: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so the side is 4 cm.
Second cube: Each edge is 64 cm. To find the volume, write 64³ cm³: 64 × 64 × 64 = 4096 × 64 = 262144.

[MathExample] 6 Cube a sum or add two cubes
(a) Use a calculator to evaluate each pair:
(i) (1 + 2)³ and 1³ + 2³
(ii) (2 + 3)³ and 2³ + 3³
(iii) (3 + 5)³ and 3³ + 5³
(iv) (4 + 6)³ and 4³ + 6³
(b) What do you notice about the results?
(c) Which statements are true?
(i) (3 + 5)³ > 3³ + 5³
(ii) (3 + 5)³ ≠ 3³ + 5³
(iii) (3 + 5)³ < 3³ + 5³
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE079-PANEL01
[PanelIdentifier] PANEL CH01-PAGE079-PANEL02
[PanelMetadata] SOURCE: Teaching block T1.5 | 6 Cube a sum or add two cubes
[PanelSection] NON-PRINTING CARRIED PRODUCTION CONTEXT
[PanelMetadata] SOURCE: Teaching block T1.5 | APPLIES TO: CH01-PAGE079-PANEL02; assigned teaching material
[PanelContextCopy] Visual requirements. Use the supplied mathematical diagrams and all figure instructions below. No character required except the specifically identified companion insets. No scenic background required behind lesson text, tables or diagrams. Keep exact labels, dimensions, units, root-bar scope and counts. Question visuals stay distinct from solution visuals; preserve blanks until the answer. All prose in the teaching stream is friendly teacher narration addressed to the reader.
[PanelContextCopy] Keep together. Retain each Example, Try, activity, Practice or Revision question with its associated working and needed figures in this reading order. Keep a worked equation chain readable as one calculation. Do not place a side quote between a question and its answer; the specified inset positions follow completed items.
[PanelBoundary] END NON-PRINTING CARRIED PRODUCTION CONTEXT
[PanelSection] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
[AnswerLead] Check your method
(a)(i) Brackets make us add 1 + 2 first in the first expression. In the second expression, cube 1 and 2 separately:
[Equation] (1 + 2)³ = 3³ = 27
[Equation] 1³ + 2³ = 1 + 8 = 9
Use the same distinction for the other pairs:
[Equation] (ii) (2 + 3)³ = 5³ = 125;   2³ + 3³ = 8 + 27 = 35
[Equation] (iii) (3 + 5)³ = 8³ = 512;   3³ + 5³ = 27 + 125 = 152
[Equation] (iv) (4 + 6)³ = 10³ = 1000;   4³ + 6³ = 64 + 216 = 280
(b) In every pair here, cubing the sum gives a greater result than adding the separate cubes. These are different calculations, so we must not swap one for the other.
(c) We found 512 and 152. Since 512 > 152 and 512 ≠ 152, statements (i) and (ii) are true. Statement (iii) is false.

[MathExample] 7 Put in the brackets
Insert brackets to make this calculation correct:
[Equation] 6³ − 16 ÷ 2² + 6 = 56
[AnswerLead] Check your method
We must keep the numbers and signs in their original order. First find the powers: 6³ = 216 and 2² = 4. We want to group part of 216 − 16 ÷ 4 + 6 so that the result is 56.
Let’s try working backwards from 56. If the last step is +6, we need 56 − 6 = 50 before it. To get 50 by dividing by 4, we need 50 × 4 = 200. Can the earlier numbers make 200? Yes: 216 − 16 = 200.
So put brackets around 6³ − 16:
[Equation] (6³ − 16) ÷ 2² + 6 = (216 − 16) ÷ 4 + 6
[Equation] = 200 ÷ 4 + 6 = 50 + 6 = 56
The brackets make 216 − 16 happen before the division by 4. Our final 56 confirms that they are in the right place.
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE080-PANEL01

[AnswerLead] Check your method
Find the edge of each complete cube from its volume:
[Equation] Large cube edge: ∛64 = 4 cm
[Equation] Removed cube edge: ∛8 = 2 cm
Look at the marked horizontal edge. The original full width was 4 cm; the removed corner uses 2 cm of that width. The remaining part is:
[Equation] 4 − 2 = 2 cm
So the missing length is 2 cm. Subtracting the volumes, 64 − 8 = 56 cm³, would find the remaining space, not this edge length.
[SmallCaption] The lengths used in the subtraction
[Production] Production note V16. Retain the viewpoint, recess geometry and unknown-segment location specified in Production note V15 in Teaching block T1.5. Add a full-width dimension of 4 cm below the front face, a removed-width dimension of 2 cm over the recess, and label the original unknown segment 2 cm. Do not move the question mark to a different edge while answering. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.

[MathSection] Chapter 01 Key Ideas
Here are the ideas you will need for the revision. Use these reminders, then try choosing the methods yourself.
[MathSubsection] Four operations on integers
On a number line, adding a positive amount moves right; subtracting a positive amount moves left:
[Equation] 6 + 4 = 10;   8 − 5 = 3
Adding a negative moves left; subtracting a negative moves right:
[Equation] 2 + (−3) = 2 − 3 = −1
[Equation] 2 − (−3) = 2 + 3 = 5
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE084-PANEL01

[PanelSection] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
For multiplication and division of non-zero numbers, different signs give a negative answer; same signs give a positive answer:
[Equation] 3 × (−2) = −(3 × 2) = −6
[Equation] −3 × 2 = −(3 × 2) = −6
[Equation] 64 ÷ (−4) = −(64 ÷ 4) = −16
[Equation] (−64) ÷ 4 = −(64 ÷ 4) = −16
For matching signs: (−3) × (−2) = 6 and (−12) ÷ (−3) = 4.
Check a division by multiplying the answer by the divisor. For example, (−16) × (−4) = 64 checks 64 ÷ (−4) = −16.

[MathSubsection] Order of operations
When several operations share an expression, use this order:
1. Work inside brackets first, starting with the innermost brackets. Follow these same rules inside them.
2. Find powers and roots.
3. Multiply and divide from left to right.
4. Add and subtract from left to right.
Multiplication and division share a place in the queue. Do whichever comes first from the left:
[Equation] 12 ÷ 3 × 2 = 4 × 2 = 8
Division comes first in that example. Addition and subtraction also share a place:
[Equation] 10 − 7 + 2 = 3 + 2 = 5
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE085-PANEL01

Now put the rules together. First work out the bracket, 7 + 8 = 15:
[Equation] 3 + 8 ÷ 2² + (7 + 8) − 9 × 2
[Equation] = 3 + 8 ÷ 2² + 15 − 9 × 2
[Equation] = 3 + 8 ÷ 4 + 15 − 9 × 2
[Equation] = 3 + 2 + 15 − 18
[Equation] = 5 + 15 − 18
[Equation] = 20 − 18 = 2
After the bracket, find 2² = 4. Then 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 9 × 2 = 18. Finally, add and subtract from the left.

[MathSubsection] Squares and square roots
Squaring multiplies a number by itself. A square root reverses that operation; the √ sign gives the root that is positive or zero:
[Equation] 4² = 4 × 4 = 16
[Equation] √144 = √(12 × 12) = 12
[MathSubsection] Cubes and cube roots
Cubing uses three equal factors. A cube root finds the repeated factor:
[Equation] 8³ = 8 × 8 × 8 = 512
[Equation] ∛729 = ∛(9 × 9 × 9) = 9

[PanelSection] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
[MathSubsection] Lowest common multiple and highest common factor
The LCM is the smallest positive shared multiple. For 6 and 8:
[Equation] Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, …
[Equation] Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, …
The common multiples begin 24, 48, …, so LCM(6, 8) = 24. “Lowest” and “least” mean the same thing here.
The HCF is the greatest positive shared factor. Factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3, 6. Factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4, 8. Their common factors are 1 and 2, so HCF(6, 8) = 2.
For a first shared total or return time, look for an LCM. For the greatest number of equal packs, or the largest piece that fits exactly, look for an HCF.
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE086-PANEL01

[MathSubsection] Divisibility tests
For 2, check for a last digit of 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. For 3 or 9, add the digits and check whether the sum divides exactly by 3 or 9. For 4, check the last two digits; for 8, the last three. For 5, the last digit must be 0 or 5. For 6, pass both the 2-test and 3-test.
For 7, double the last digit and subtract it from the remaining number; repeat if needed. For 10, the last digit must be 0. For 25, the last two digits must be 00, 25, 50 or 75. For 100, the last two digits must be 00.

[MathSection] Chapter 01 Revision
Have a go before looking at the working. If you get stuck, name the job first: a change in position, a shared multiple, a shared factor, a divisibility check, or a power or root. Choosing the job is part of solving the question.
[MathExample] 1 Evaluate
(a) 7 + (−3) (b) −6 + (−5) (c) 17 − (−2) (d) −6 − (−3)
[AnswerLead] Check your method
[Equation] (a) 7 + (−3) = 7 − 3 = 4
[Equation] (b) −6 + (−5) = −6 − 5 = −11
[Equation] (c) 17 − (−2) = 17 + 2 = 19
[Equation] (d) −6 − (−3) = −6 + 3 = −3

[MathExample] 2 Evaluate
(a) −11 + 5 − 8 (b) 120 − 80 − 50 (c) −15 × 8
(d) 64 ÷ (−16) (e) (−82 − 18) ÷ 4 − 12
(f) [32 − (−49 ÷ 7) × 4] + 80
[AnswerLead] Check your method
[Equation] (a) −11 + 5 − 8 = −6 − 8 = −14
[Equation] (b) 120 − 80 − 50 = 40 − 50 = −10
[Equation] (c) −15 × 8 = −(15 × 8) = −120
[Equation] (d) 64 ÷ (−16) = −(64 ÷ 16) = −4
[Equation] (e) (−82 − 18) ÷ 4 − 12 = −100 ÷ 4 − 12 = −25 − 12 = −37
(f) There are brackets inside brackets. Start with −49 ÷ 7 = −7. Inside the square brackets, multiply −7 × 4 before subtracting:
[Equation] [32 − (−49 ÷ 7) × 4] + 80
[Equation] = [32 − (−7) × 4] + 80
[Equation] = [32 − (−28)] + 80
[Equation] = [32 + 28] + 80
[Equation] = 60 + 80 = 140
The subtraction of −28 becomes addition of 28. Keeping the brackets until that point makes the two minus signs easier to follow.

[PanelSection] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
[MathExample] 3 Fire alarms
Three fire alarms go off every 3 minutes, 5 minutes and 8 minutes. They first go off together at 10 a.m. When will all three next go off together?
[AnswerLead] Check your method
We need the first shared wait, so use an LCM. Multiples of both 3 and 5 are 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, 120, … . The first of these also divisible by 8 is 120:
[Equation] 120 ÷ 3 = 40;   120 ÷ 5 = 24;   120 ÷ 8 = 15
None of the earlier times in that list divides by 8 exactly. So we wait 120 ÷ 60 = 2 hours. 10 a.m. + 2 hours = 12 p.m., or noon.
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE088-PANEL01

[AnswerLead] Check your method
(a) A cube’s side must fit exactly along all three lengths: 30 cm, 18 cm and 12 cm. Find their HCF.
Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Those that also divide both 18 and 30 are 1, 2, 3 and 6. The greatest is 6, so each cube has side length 6 cm.
(b) Count cubes along, across and up:
[Equation] Along the 30 cm length: 30 ÷ 6 = 5
[Equation] Along the 12 cm depth: 12 ÷ 6 = 2
[Equation] Along the 18 cm height: 18 ÷ 6 = 3
[Equation] Total: 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 cubes
[SmallCaption] Five by two by three cubes
[Production] Production note V18. Repeat the source orientation and show a 5-column, 2-deep, 3-high partition. Add one separate layer plan with exactly 5 by 2 cells labelled 10 cubes in one layer. Label 3 layers and a unit edge of 6 cm. The completed cuboid contains 30 cubes, including those hidden from view. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
One layer holds 5 × 2 = 10 cubes, and there are 3 layers. That gives 30 cubes, not 5 + 2 + 3.

[MathExample] 5 Use divisibility tests
Check whether each number is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 25 and 100.
(a) 504  (b) 12345678
[AnswerLead] Check your method
(a) The digit sum of 504 is 5 + 0 + 4 = 9. For 7, use 50 − 2 × 4 = 42, which is divisible by 7.
(b) The digit sum of 12345678 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 36. Its 7-test goes:
[Equation] 1234567 − 2 × 8 = 1234551
[Equation] 123455 − 2 × 1 = 123453
[Equation] 12345 − 2 × 3 = 12339
[Equation] 1233 − 2 × 9 = 1215
[Equation] 121 − 2 × 5 = 111
[Equation] 11 − 2 × 1 = 9
9 is not divisible by 7, so 12345678 fails that test.

[MathExample] 6 Find the smallest shared multiple
Write down the smallest number divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 25 and 100.
[AnswerLead] Check your method
Here “smallest” means the smallest positive number, as in our LCM work. This looks like eleven separate jobs, but some are already covered by others.
Start with 100: 100 ÷ 2 = 50, 100 ÷ 4 = 25, 100 ÷ 5 = 20, 100 ÷ 10 = 10 and 100 ÷ 25 = 4. So every multiple of 100 already fits those five divisors.
A multiple of 9 also divides by 3, because 9 = 3 × 3. If it is also even, it passes the 6-test. That leaves us looking for the first shared multiple of 100, 8, 9 and 7.
First fit 100 and 8. Try 100, then 200:
[Equation] 100 = 8 × 12 + 4
[Equation] 200 = 8 × 25
100 leaves 4 over; 200 divides exactly. So the LCM of 100 and 8 is 200. Their shared multiples are 200, 400, 600, ….

[MathExample] 8 Compare the roots
Fill each blank with < or >. What do you notice?
(a) √64 □ ∛64 (b) √729 □ ∛729
(c) √70 □ ∛70 (d) ∛65 □ √65
[AnswerLead] Check your method
(a) √64 = 8 and ∛64 = 4. Since 8 > 4, √64 > ∛64.
(b) √729 = 27 because 27² = 729; ∛729 = 9 because 9³ = 729. Since 27 > 9, √729 > ∛729.
(c) 70 is not a perfect square or cube. Let’s trap each root between numbers we know.
For √70, 8 × 8 = 64 is too small and 9 × 9 = 81 is too large. So √70 lies between 8 and 9.
For ∛70, 4³ = 64 is too small and 5³ = 125 is too large. So ∛70 lies between 4 and 5.
Anything between 8 and 9 is greater than anything between 4 and 5. Therefore √70 > ∛70.
(d) Use the same nearby powers for 65: 4³ = 64 < 65 < 125 = 5³, while 8² = 64 < 65 < 81 = 9². So ∛65 is between 4 and 5, and √65 is between 8 and 9. The cube root comes first here, so ∛65 < √65.
In all four examples, the square root is greater than the cube root. This comparison holds for numbers greater than 1. It is not a rule for every number: at 1 the two roots are equal, for example.
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE094-PANEL02

[MathExample] 9 Work without a calculator
Calculate (a) 13 + 2 × 5², (b) (2³ − 12) × 4 and (c) 6 − (10 − 4²).
[AnswerLead] Check your method
[Equation] (a) 13 + 2 × 5² = 13 + 2 × 25 = 13 + 50 = 63
[Equation] (b) (2³ − 12) × 4 = (8 − 12) × 4 = (−4) × 4 = −16
[Equation] (c) 6 − (10 − 4²) = 6 − (10 − 16) = 6 − (−6) = 12
In (c), working inside the brackets still means doing 4² before 10 − 16. The last step subtracts a negative, so 6 − (−6) = 6 + 6 = 12.

[MathSubsection] A final check of your understanding
Here are four extra questions. This time, tell me why your method works as well as finding the answer. Try them before reading the responses.
A. Explain a sign. A friend says −4 − (−7) = −11. What has your friend misunderstood? Give the correct working.
B. Choose a method. Two lights flash every 6 and 10 seconds. Do you use HCF or LCM to find their next shared flash after starting together? Why?
C. Apply an idea. A square has area 81 cm² and a cube has volume 125 cm³. Find one side of each. Write the units.
D. Check a claim. A friend says 3² + 4² = 7². Check both sides and explain the mistake.
[PanelBoundary] END PANEL CH01-PAGE096-PANEL01
[PanelIdentifier] PANEL CH01-PAGE096-PANEL02
[PanelMetadata] SOURCE: Teaching block R01 | A final check of your understanding
[PanelSection] NON-PRINTING CARRIED PRODUCTION CONTEXT
[PanelMetadata] SOURCE: Teaching block R01 | APPLIES TO: CH01-PAGE096-PANEL02; assigned teaching material
[PanelContextCopy] Visual requirements. Use the supplied mathematical diagrams and all figure instructions below. No character required except the specifically identified companion insets. No scenic background required behind lesson text, tables or diagrams. Keep exact labels, dimensions, units, root-bar scope and counts. Question visuals stay distinct from solution visuals; preserve blanks until the answer. All prose in the teaching stream is friendly teacher narration addressed to the reader.
[PanelContextCopy] Keep together. Retain each Example, Try, activity, Practice or Revision question with its associated working and needed figures in this reading order. Keep a worked equation chain readable as one calculation. Do not place a side quote between a question and its answer; the specified inset positions follow completed items.
[PanelBoundary] END NON-PRINTING CARRIED PRODUCTION CONTEXT
[PanelSection] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
[AnswerLead] Check your understanding
A. The second minus sign belongs to −7. Subtracting −7 means adding 7, not subtracting 7: −4 − (−7) = −4 + 7 = 3. Check: 3 + (−7) = −4.
B. Use the LCM, because the waiting time must be a whole number of both 6-second and 10-second intervals. Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30; multiples of 10 are 10, 20, 30. The first shared flash is 30 seconds later.
C. Square side: √81 = 9 cm, since 9 × 9 = 81. Cube side: ∛125 = 5 cm, since 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. Both answers are lengths, so both use cm.
D. 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, but 7² = 49. The friend added 3 + 4 before squaring, even though the original calculation asks for two separate squares.
If one response was difficult, revisit that method and try the question again with the answer covered. You are ready to move on when you can explain the choice, show the working and make a sensible check without copying the solution.

[ProductionContextSource] Carried forward from Reading this manuscript — state and visual ownership | Applies to: Assigned visual beats and companion insets
[ProductionContextCopy] The scene’s Setting, View, Cast and Props describe its shared setup and state progression. The visual beats specify the state at each individual moment; do not show a later result in an earlier beat. A change of speaker or physical action may require a new visual, but a source paragraph break or a short attribution such as “Tara explains” does not create one by itself. A brief confirmation and the rest of one continuous explanation may share a speaking beat where explicitly stated.
[ProductionContextSource] Carried forward from Reading this manuscript — printable field ownership | Applies to: Assigned printable fields
[ProductionContextCopy] Pagination, panelisation and page production must preserve these field boundaries. Compare each completed balloon with its SPEECH BUBBLE TEXT field: no added speaker label or instruction is permitted. A character name that is part of the approved spoken line must remain. These rules also apply to all companion-inset balloons. Story scene and visual-beat headings are production references; teaching headings and teaching content retain their existing printable status.
[ProductionContextSource] Carried forward from Lantern Street Cube Plinth, Handle and Moonline Joint — location instructions | Applies to: Assigned beats of Scene CH01 10B; Assigned beats of Scene CH01 10C
[ProductionContextCopy] A low square plinth under an indigo canopy stands opposite the mirror. The five-indicator wall control and large down-pull handle are on its right. One flat brass cover lies in the paving at the plinth’s front-right corner, over the moonline joint.
[ProductionContextCopy] Sixty-four small lantern cubes form one solid 4 × 4 × 4 block between the square base and top frame. The failed state is uneven narrow towers. An exact layer diagram shows sixteen cubes, then four layers. The final handle stays separate from the floor cover. Under that cover are two disconnected track ends, screws and black dust; there is no hidden second switch. The joint repair, not another calculation, makes the final light flow.
[ProductionContextCopy] Required views. Medium plinth; exact single layer and complete cube inserts; hand-on-handle still; low disconnected/connected joint views; result wide belongs to Lantern Street.
[ProductionContextEnd] END NON-PRINTING PRODUCTION CONTEXT
## Scene CH01 10B Everyone clear
[SourceLocator] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[SceneInstruction] Setting. Lantern Street cube plinth and final control. A low square plinth beneath an indigo canopy stands opposite the mirror. The five-indicator wall control and large down-pull handle are on its right. A separate flat brass cover in the paving at the plinth’s front-right corner hides the right-edge moonline joint. Blue wall, canopy post and paving seam fix the geography. Same full-moon night in Mumbai. Warm fixed work lamps and the portable brass lamp make faces and hands readable; cool moonlight edges roofs and canopy gaps. Main lantern arches remain dark unless this scene explicitly changes them.
[SceneInstruction] View. Medium from the mirror side towards the right-side control and separate floor cover.
[SceneInstruction] Cast and staging across the scene. Ahana steps to the large down-pull handle. Tara asks the others to move clear with an open-hand gesture; her staff remains leaned safely against the wall. Vihaan and Navya step onto clear paving behind Ahana. Tez and the helper are outside the handle’s movement area.
[SceneInstruction] Props and state progression. Handle still raised. All five white indicators, completed cube and mirror. Work lamp stands where Ahana left it, outside the walking line. Floor cover closed.
[SceneInstruction] Planning requirements. This precedes the first handle action. Nobody stands under a loose part; the fittings themselves have been secured.

## Scene CH01 10E Following the moonline
[SourceLocator] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[SceneInstruction] Setting. Lantern Street cube plinth and final control. A low square plinth beneath an indigo canopy stands opposite the mirror. The five-indicator wall control and large down-pull handle are on its right. A separate flat brass cover in the paving at the plinth’s front-right corner hides the right-edge moonline joint. Blue wall, canopy post and paving seam fix the geography. Same full-moon night in Mumbai. Warm fixed work lamps and the portable brass lamp make faces and hands readable; cool moonlight edges roofs and canopy gaps. Main lantern arches remain dark unless this scene explicitly changes them.

# Sequence 11 The signature and the next street
[SourceLocator] Production sequence reference CH01-11. The following location descriptions are retained from V16.
### Lantern Street Square Mirror Recess
[SceneInstruction] A shallow square brass frame stands just above the paving in an alcove on the far-left wall. A blue rear wall, a warm lamp on the left and an open canopy gap identify it. A padded tray and opaque tile crate sit outside the walking lane.
[SceneInstruction] The inventory is 81 equal, unbroken square mirror tiles. The helper empties the mislaid arrangement before the mathematical layout. The exact result is one flat 9 × 9 grid, reflecting one continuous full moon. The inner brass rim carries a V hidden in dust until the arches light. Keep that rim, lamp, crate and paving seam consistent. A diagram supplies the count; a wide image need not reveal every tile.
[SceneInstruction] Required views. Medium empty-frame setup; high three-quarter exact grid after teaching; separate Tez reflection view; later rim-and-V close-up from the same frame.
### Old Blue Gate Exterior Waiting Lane
[SceneInstruction] Two enormous weathered blue timber doors stand between pale-stone piers. Brass ribs and moon-shaped openings decorate the doors. A round full-moon ornament hangs above. Seen from outside, a small service door is cut into the left door leaf. A bench is on the right and a planter on the left.
[SceneInstruction] The separate equipment exit is farther left beyond the stone pier. It is not the child-height door in the large leaf. Children aged eight to thirteen wait in contemporary urban casual clothing. Use a few foreground groups and a suggested crowd; do not render three hundred individually countable people. Ira, Kabir and the girl in green remain identifiable. Tara does not meet the trio outside. The Bell is never mounted on the Gate arch.
[SceneInstruction] Required views. Arrival wide from the lane; bench/planter medium; invitation close-up; low Tez doorway view. Gate ornaments and invitations have bright, fading and restored-light states without changing their shapes.
### Food Street Master from Lantern Street
[SceneInstruction] A covered lane beneath saffron and teal awnings opens beyond Lantern Street’s shutters. The recipe and cooking counter is on the left; jugs and the juice urn are on the right. The near packing bench has a side door to Return Walk. A round two-tray loading table sits in the central clear lane.
[SceneInstruction] The far opening leads to the Parade Ground. The initial obstruction is one crooked cart with a bowl under its wheel. The food helper wears a saffron apron and ivory cap; two smaller assistants deliver food. The main cooking surface is behind the counter, beyond the children’s hands. The sixteen-cup trolley waits at the packing end. No human cooks or hidden extra kitchen are introduced.
[SceneInstruction] Required views. Threshold wide; separate recipe, drinks and packing counter views; central loading-table medium. The waiting Gate crowd is shown in its own cutaway, never behind the cooking counter.
## Scene CH01 11A A mark in the mirror rim
[SourceLocator] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[SceneInstruction] Setting. Lantern Street square-mirror recess. A shallow square brass frame sits just above paving in the far-left wall alcove, opposite the cube plinth. The rear wall is blue, the warm lamp is on the left, and a canopy gap admits moonlight. The padded tray and opaque crate stay outside the walking lane. The inner rim and paving seam remain fixed across views. Same full-moon night after the joint repair. Golden arch light fills Lantern Street; the moonline is continuous. Warm work lamps remain, with cool moonlight on roofs and the mirror. This repair does not restore Tez’s stripes or ring the Moon Bell.
[SceneInstruction] View. Close on the inner brass mirror rim specified under Setting in Scene CH01 11A, now caught by restored golden arch light. Keep the left lamp and a corner of the exact tile grid as anchors.

Vihaan and Navya approach from the plinth side. Tara places the lamp on stable paving beside the mirror and comes to inspect; the helper remains near the plinth.
[SceneInstruction] Props and state progression. First readable V scratched in the dusty inner brass rim. Mirror still 9 × 9 with unbroken tiles. The original dusty card remains inside its one paper sleeve; it is not a new clue card.

## Scene CH01 11C A little hope outside
[SourceLocator] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[SceneInstruction] Setting. Old Blue Gate exterior waiting lane in Mumbai. Two enormous weathered blue timber doors stand between pale-stone piers, with brass ribs, moon-shaped openings and one round full-moon ornament above. Seen from outside, the small service door is in the left door leaf, the planter is left and the bench right. The separate equipment exit lies farther left beyond the pier. Same full-moon night, simultaneous with the restored street. Ira’s invitation and the round Gate ornament brighten against the Mumbai lane. The blue doors stay closed; nearby warm lamps keep the waiting children readable.
[SceneInstruction] View. Independent exterior cutaway facing the Old Blue Gate from the Mumbai lane. Retain the tall blue doors, pale piers, round moon ornament, left planter and right bench specified under Setting in Scene CH01 11C.
[SceneInstruction] Cast and staging across the scene. Ira in her pale powder-blue jacket holds up her invitation and shows it to Kabir, who leans slightly towards it in his rust hoodie. They then look up at the brightening ornament; separate stills may show these two gazes. The green-waistcoated Gate helper stands by the small service door. Modern child visitor groups wait nearby, including the green-hoodie girl with her friends. The trio, Tara and Tez are inside and not visible here.
[SceneInstruction] Props and state progression. Ira’s same silver crescent invitation glows again. The full-moon ornament brightens. Main Gate doors remain closed; this is not admission or the welcome ring. Kabir has his slim notebook; he is not yet counting an admitted group.
[SceneInstruction] Planning requirements. No off-frame inside dialogue over this cutaway. The outside children see a hopeful change but do not know about the V or Veer. Do not place the exterior crowd behind the solid interior map wall.

# Source and addition record
[SourceLocator] Production record only. None of this section is learner copy.
## Revision and planning clarity
V02 applies the author’s 19 October 2026 correction: every human character has fair skin. This supersedes the older skin descriptions for this manuscript while preserving names, faces, ages, hair, clothes, actions and dialogue. Tez’s fur and the wooden helpers’ material stay as established.
All 60 scenes have been reviewed for drawable moments and exact text ownership. Repeated full speaking beats use separate visual beats with an explicit pose or expression change and fixed location continuity. Short attributions stay with their associated speech as non-printing speaker metadata and do not require their own image. One continuous confirmation and explanation in 02A is deliberately kept together. Scene 01D now shows the helper below, followed by two matching street-level images of Tara speaking; Scene 01E uses one visual for both source narration paragraphs.
Bare source-element numbers have been removed from scene instructions. They were internal audit locators, not source page numbers, graphic-novel pages or panel assignments. Stable scene identifiers and visual-beat letters now provide the references a planner needs. The source comparison is recorded below; no learner words were deleted to simplify the labels.
V03 changes only the authorised treatment of speech attributions and printable text fields. All 82 dialogue fields, including eleven companion quotes, now separate non-printing speaker and tail metadata from balloon text. Thirty-six bare attribution captions and three attribution phrases are retained in that metadata. The two associated actions remain captions: “Ahana catches the handle. She lifts the lamp higher.” and “Vihaan follows the strip with his finger.” The location lead-in remains “In Lantern Street…”. Spoken words, their order and visual-beat assignments are unchanged; only outer prose quotation marks and attribution commas are adapted for balloons. All other story, teaching, locations, staging, props and pose instructions remain unchanged.
## Sources and scope
Story source: CHANDRUSH-DETAILED-BOOK-WISE-STORY-V-16(3).docx. The complete book-wide STORY stream, global descriptions and reveal/timing record informed continuity. Only Chapter 01 story paragraphs are carried into this manuscript. All Chapter 01 detailed location descriptions and relevant Gate descriptions are retained before their sequences.
Teaching source: CH01-FRIENDLY-TEACHER-STUDY-MATERIAL-DRAFT-10(3).docx, supplied by the author for this integration. Its original title is Chapter 01 Numbers; its descriptor is Friendly Teacher Study Material; its status line is Draft 10 · Review Draft — Awaiting approval. This integration does not claim a separate approval of that teaching draft.
The teaching source’s learner content is carried over once in full, in its original order, with its eight tables, twenty embedded diagrams, production notes and native mathematical notation. Its original end production notes are retained below. No example names, objects, values, methods, units or answers have been substituted.
Visual references reviewed: the five supplied character sheets and the relevant Chapter 01 location views. V16 controls current geography, mechanisms and states. Earlier location imagery differs in the timing drums, blue clips, supply shutters, controls and floor mirror, so those obsolete content details are not imported. Tez’s written blue-to-pale stripe state controls the colour while the sheet supplies his face, proportions and scarf.
## Boundary decisions
T1.1A ends immediately before Taking away a negative amount. Draft 10 combines introductory addition and subtraction in its earlier number-line material and paired pattern table. Those passages remain intact in T1.1A; T1.1B carries the separately headed negative-subtraction treatment. This follows V16’s instruction to adjust internal boundaries without reordering the teaching.
T1.1C carries multiplication, division, inverse checks and all Practice 1A, including its bracket task. The full mixed-operation consolidation is not in that early source span; it remains in Chapter 01 Key Ideas at R01, with the powers and roots it uses. No section has been moved forward, duplicated or invented.
T1.2A stops before Factors. T1.2B preserves Examples 9, 10 and 11 in their original HCF, LCM, HCF order. R01 retains everything after Section 1.5 through the final understanding response. There is no separately titled performance task in Draft 10 to add.
